title: Do You Know It, Can You Do It, Do You Show It?
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that organisations routinely lump knowledge, skills and behaviours into a single vague idea of capability, and that this confusion wastes training budgets and muddies feedback. She separates the three layers with a question each: do you know what matters, can you actually do it, and do you show it consistently. Knowledge is the easiest to fake, skills require practice and decay without use, and behaviours are the visible, repeated evidence that others actually judge. The move is diagnostic: she gives a simple test for telling a knowledge gap from a skill gap from a behaviour gap, so a leader can intervene at the point where the chain actually breaks. She closes by asking readers to locate their own sticking point.
points: Knowledge, skills and behaviours answer different questions, and treating them as synonyms leads to courses heavy on slides and light on practice or reinforcement.
Knowledge is easy to fake with buzzwords, so recognising terms is not evidence that someone can apply them.
Skills need practice and feedback and atrophy faster than knowledge, so one-off training does not hold.
A behaviour is proven by consistent repetition under pressure, not by a single demonstration, which is why it exposes the gap between what teams say they value and what they reward.
A quick diagnostic (can talk but not apply, can apply but not under pressure, can do but does not consistently show) tells a leader which layer to strengthen.
quotes: Knowledge is embodied by the theories, concepts, facts and mental models we draw on to make sense of a situation. Without knowledge, we’re guessing.
Unlike knowledge, skills can’t be acquired by reading. They require practice, feedback and a commitment to continuous improvement.
Skills also degrade without use. You might once have been fluent in a coding language or adept at public speaking, but if you don’t keep applying those skills, they slowly fade (at least to a point).
One act of listening doesn’t make you an active listener. The behaviour is only credible when it shows up reliably, across situations, especially under pressure.
Training budgets get wasted: We deliver courses heavy on slides (knowledge) but light on practice (skills) or reinforcement (behaviours).
Growth comes from tracing where the chain breaks - between knowing, doing and showing - and strengthening it there.
